claim: This 2005 foundational handbook chapter provides decision-grade evidence for classical vocabulary, analytical lineage and boundary conditions: interaction control regulates mechanical-port behavior; impedance maps motion to force, admittance maps force to motion, and coupled stability depends on the exact robot–environment feedback interconnection rather than isolated controller stability. It is tutorial/review-level evidence and does not establish modern experimental performance, deployment safety or learning-controller guarantees.
claim_locator: Force feedback, natural admittance and series elasticity
epistemic_status: foundational handbook tutorial/review synthesis for definitions, classical analytical results, mechanism lineage and boundaries only
problem_and_setting: Controlling physical interaction through a mechanical port where robot and environment form a dynamically coupled feedback system.
method_or_mechanism: Uses impedance/admittance causality and classical passivity analysis; treats robot and environment as an exact feedback interconnection; discusses direct impedance, force-feedback apparent-inertia reduction, natural admittance and series springs/dampers.
content_summary: Counterexamples show isolated-stable motion or force controllers becoming unstable after environmental mass or spring coupling. Passive power-continuous port interconnection is a classical sufficient stability framework, with strict passivity supporting asymptotic behavior. Constant-reference simple impedance can be passive, but sampling and unmodeled dynamics can break it. Force feedback lowers apparent inertia/friction but resonance, delay and noncollocation can make gains above unity nonpassive. Natural admittance retains physical inertia; series compliance filters the environment at bandwidth/accuracy cost. Pure motion/force are infinite/zero-impedance ideals.
synthesis_role: Defines the classical port vocabulary and coupled-stability baseline for classifying later variable, optimization and learning methods.
development_link: Foundational precursor to variable impedance, energy tanks, passivity observers, SEA, sampled-data interaction control and learned policy stability analysis.

evidence.finding: Isolated-stable controllers can become unstable when coupled to environmental mass or stiffness.
Impedance maps motion to force, admittance maps force to motion, and the interconnection is exact feedback.
Passive robot/environment ports under power-continuous coupling are stable under stated conditions; strict passivity on one side supports asymptotic stability.
A nonpassive robot port can be destabilized by a selected passive spring or mass.
Constant-reference low-friction torque implementation can be passive, but sampling and unmodeled dynamics may destroy passivity.
It reduces apparent inertia/friction, while resonance, delay and noncollocation can make high gain nonpassive.
They preserve inertia or mechanically filter interaction, trading bandwidth and position accuracy for robustness.

boundary_conditions: Most results concern classical LTI one-port low-order settings.
Passivity assumes power-conjugate variables and power-continuous coupling.
Sampling, delay, resonance and noncollocation can invalidate continuous-time passivity.
Active humans, powered tools, switched, delayed and multi-contact systems require more analysis.
The 2005 chapter does not cover modern learning, MPC or collaborative standards.
assumptions: Compatible mechanical-port variables represent the system.
Passivity holds for realized systems, not just ideal models.
Strict-passivity conditions hold for asymptotic conclusions.
Omitted implementation dynamics are benign or separately analyzed.

reported: Isolated stability can fail after coupling.
Nonpassive ports can be destabilized by passive environments.
Sampling and unmodeled dynamics may break passivity.
High force-feedback gain can become nonpassive.
Series compliance reduces bandwidth and accuracy.
inferred: Classical one-port results do not directly guarantee learned, hybrid, delayed or multi-contact systems.
Passivity is conditional coupled stability, not universal deployment safety.
Tutorial evidence cannot establish modern method superiority.
